source.title: Constructing Interpretable Features from Compositional Neuron Groups
source.authors: O. Shafran; Atticus Geiger; Mor Geva

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies compositional neuron groups, but does not measure the share of interpretable neuron poles, test the classic examples or architecture estimates, evaluate explanation prediction scores, or construct attribution graphs. Its neuron-group results do not establish whether the listed claim versions hold.
record.gate_note: The paper reports concept-detection and steering results for SNMF features, but those method benchmarks do not measure any listed version. The included rows cover its explicit neuron-subset interventions and its parent–child feature causal-coverage analysis; these concern neuron-group composition but do not test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper builds SNMF features from groups of co-activated MLP neurons and studies how they compose. It never audits individual neuron poles for share of interpretable jobs, tests InceptionV1 examples, estimates interpretable shares across tools or architectures, builds neuron attribution graphs, or scores single-neuron explanations by simulation. It cites neuron polysemanticity only as motivation for moving to directions. Its concept-detection and steering scores belong to SNMF features, not neurons, so they do not bear on V6 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors conclude that SNMF finds interpretable MLP features as sparse neuron combinations, which outperform SAEs and DiffMeans at steering and match SAEs on detection. They also conclude that neuron groups compose additively into hierarchical concepts, which explains why the same neurons join multiple features.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SNMF on MLP activations to extract sparse neuron combinations and tests feature detection, steering, and composition; it does not reproduce the neuron-pole audit or explanation-scoring procedures in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across model layers and SNMF settings: concept detection can decline with larger k in some layers; causal steering and fluency differ across layers; intervention results also depend on which neuron subset is amplified.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-2 Large, amplifying the neurons shared across weekday features raises every weekday logit by 4.7 to 6.0. Amplifying one day's exclusive neurons promotes that day's token and mostly suppresses the others.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantically related MLP features share a core neuron set, with exclusive neurons that specialise fine-grained concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: Parent SNMF features cover child-promoted tokens well above a random-pairing control: 0.46 vs 0.05 in Llama-3.1 8B and 0.37 vs 0.00 in Gemma-2 2B. Child diversity stays about 0.99.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLP neuron-group features form broad-to-specific hierarchies whose parents cover their children's causal effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Over 75% of SNMF features score positive on concept detection. SNMF features steer better than SAEs and often match or beat DiffMeans. These are scores for neuron-combination features, not single neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse neuron-group features from MLP activations are more causally effective units than SAE features.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper does not test the listed claim versions. It notes that benchmarks used feature counts k < 500, that LLM-as-judge results may be sensitive to prompt and evaluation details, and that its human check was based on 50 judged examples.
record.rows_left_out: Left out concept-detection and concept-steering benchmark results and SNMF hyperparameter/initiation tables because they compare feature-extraction methods or characterize SNMF settings rather than testing a listed version of the claim.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares of one-job, two-job and unexplained neurons.
No single-neuron interpretability shares across models, architectures or scale.
No analysis of InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neurons, and no test of pose or recursive generalization against superposition.
No test of whether architecture, regularization or tools cause messy neurons, and no interpretable-share estimates.
No neuron-based attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
Explanations from activating examples are evaluated only for SNMF features (concept detection), not for individual neurons.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Row states of cannot_determine with versions ['none'] are appropriate. The paper's framing assumes neurons are polysemantic, the opposite premise to the essay, but it provides no single-neuron measurement that tests V1–V7. The Table 2 values are deltas from an implicit zero baseline, the non-intervened logits, and are read correctly.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report shares with one, two, or unknown jobs.
Does not measure those shares across models, architectures, or scale.
Does not analyze InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or test pose, recursive generalization, or superposition.
Does not test the stated causes of messy neurons or estimate interpretability shares for vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or compare them with a trained replacement model or reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on new text.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
